Action Plan:
1. Right knee pain with exercise/clicking:
   • Continue regular ice therapy after activity.  
   • Temporarily reduce running mileage; stop activity if knee pain increases.  
   • Prescription for a stronger oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) to be taken with food; do NOT combine with current ibuprofen.  
   • Physiotherapy referral arranged for detailed knee examination and rehabilitation program.  
   • Consider imaging (e.g., MRI) after physiotherapy assessment if structural injury suspected.  
   • Red-flag advice: seek urgent review for persistent swelling, heat, redness, fever, knee locking, or inability to flex/extend.

2. Follow-up / escalation:
   • GP clinic review offered if physiotherapy wait-time is excessive or symptoms worsen.  
   • Prescription sent electronically to patient’s nominated pharmacy.

Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive right knee pain and clicking during running/leg-extension exercises over the last 2 weeks; occasional toe tingling post-run.  
• Onset & course: Began after increasing long-run distance to 7–8 mi for marathon training; pain starts ~20 min (~3 mi) into run, sometimes forces cessation; improves with rest/ice.  
• Associated features: One episode of mild knee swelling that resolved with ice; no current swelling, redness, locking, giving-way, or instability. Single episode of right-toe tingling; no ongoing numbness.  
• Past medical history: Hyperopia (LASIK surgery), significant UTI/possible renal colic in past; right knee contusion from ice-hockey fall months ago.  
• Medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN; Aleve (naproxen) PRN—dose/route/frequency not documented; vitamin D; melatonin; occasional Xanax—dose/route/frequency not documented; occasional marijuana smoking (joint).  
• Allergies: Not documented.  
• Social history: Highly active (running, gym, ice hockey); lives in London; occasional marijuana use; alcohol/tobacco history not discussed.

Objective:
(Virtual consultation — no formal examination)  
• Patient reports current ability to fully flex and extend right knee without pain at rest.  
• No visible swelling at time of call; prior transient swelling noted after first painful run.  
• No warmth, erythema, or tenderness reported on self-palpation.  
• Normal gait, stair negotiation, and walking reported.  
• No calf tenderness, colour change, or persistent oedema; mild sock indentation after prolonged standing.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Right knee pain/clicking with activity  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (runner’s knee / chondromalacia patella) — DDx item, likelihood High.  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Patellar tendinopathy (Medium) – overuse pattern consistent.  
     • Meniscal tear (Medium) – prior trauma & clicking support; absence of locking/swelling argues against.  
     • Iliotibial band syndrome (Low-Medium) – lateral pain possible.  
     • Ligamentous injury (ACL/MCL sprain) (Low) – no instability; patient concern noted.  
   - Investigations planned: None immediately; consider MRI if physiotherapist suspects structural lesion.  
   - Treatment planned: Continue ice; reduce running; prescribe stronger NSAID (name/dose not documented) with food; avoid concurrent ibuprofen/naproxen.  
   - Relevant referrals: Physiotherapy for comprehensive knee assessment and rehab.

2. Episodic right-toe tingling post-run  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Likely transient nerve irritation secondary to mechanical stress/overuse.  
   - Differential diagnosis: Early neuritis vs vascular cause (e.g., post-exercise oedema); deep-vein thrombosis considered unlikely (DDx “Deep venous thrombosis” – opposing clinical picture).  
   - Investigations planned: None at present.  
   - Treatment planned: Monitor; will reassess if recurrent or persistent.  
   - Relevant referrals: None at this stage.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected elements: Allergies not documented; no formal vitals or in-person knee examination due to virtual format.  
• Internal conflicts: DDx initial summary lists “bilateral” pain; transcript clarifies pain predominates in right knee (conflict noted).  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minimal background noise; occasional conversational overlap, but clinically adequate.
